transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Nimbus SRE), Aisha Khan (Nimbus Platform), Mark Chen (Nimbus CTO)

Auto-summary: Deep technical discussion about autoscaling policies, capacity planning and benchmarking for mesh of LLM endpoints. Action items captured.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everybody thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'll kick off. Priya's our SE and she'll drive the runtime bits. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Carlos: Hey, doing good. quick calendar note i'm on east coast but joined here.
[00:10] Mark: good to be here. we want to make sure basics: predictable latency under spiky traffic and not over-provisioning for cost.
[00:18] Priya: Great. high-level agenda: autoscale models, burst handling, queueing behavior, reserved GPU sizing, kv cache warmup, batching, and quantization tradeoffs. We'll go through recommended policies and then mapping to Nimbus's current traffic.
[00:30] Aisha: cool. we run two clusters — hosted-prod in gcp us-east and a private on-prem cluster in our colo for regulated PII workloads. latency SLO is p95 < 350ms for short chat prompts (~256 tokens).
[00:45] Priya: ok that SLO is helpful. first, burst policies: Redwood supports reserved capacity with a burst pool and soft-queueing. typical pattern: reserve baseline capacity to cover 95th percentile steady traffic and configure burst pool to allow X extra concurrent slots for short periods.
[01:05] Priya: For example, baseline 8 GPUs for steady state, burst pool of 2-4 GPUs with a token bucket configured so sustained bursts above baseline are throttled or queued.
[01:15] Carlos: how do you handle queueing? we care about not blowing past the 350ms SLO — if requests queue, apparent latency increases.
[01:23] Priya: we have two levers: admission control + prioritized queueing and adaptive batch sizing. admission control can reject low-priority background requests sooner, and prioritized queueing can ensure interactive requests get dispatched first. the queueing latency target is a separate SLO — we aim to keep queue wait < 50ms for interactive path, otherwise we spin up burst nodes.
[01:45] Jordan: Also, for positive user experience, we recommend a short client-side timeout with streaming partial responses so UX doesn't appear stalled during transient queueing.
[01:52] Mark: what's the typical cold-start for a GPU to be ready to accept requests (esp on-prem)?
[01:58] Priya: Cold starts depend on model size and whether KV cache needs warmup. For a 30B quantized model, node spin-up + model load ~45-90s on-prem. With cached model layers (warm-image) it can drop to 15-30s. KV cache refill for hot prefixes depends on traffic — we can warm prefixes from recent requests, but full kv cache rebuild happens over first N requests.
[02:20] Carlos: so we need burst policy to cover that warmup window. if spin-up is 60-90s we can't rely on instant elasticity.
[02:27] Priya: Exactly. That's why Redwood recommends a two-tier strategy: reserved GPUs sized to cover baseline + short bursts, and asynchronous scale-up to bring more nodes online for sustained higher load. burst pool handles the first 30-90s gap.
[02:40] Aisha: what's suggested ratio of reserved vs burst?
[02:43] Priya: Typical is reserve 60-80% of peak concurrent requests, with burst covering remaining 20-40% depending on cost tolerance. If you have predictable daily cyclical peaks, reserve for the high percentiles (e.g., 95th) and use burst for sudden irregular spikes.
[02:58] Mark: ok that sounds reasonable. Carlos, do you have telemetry we can map?
[03:02] Carlos: Yes i'll pull 72 hours of traffic and token counts. we currently see median qps ~120, 95th ~450, spikes up to 900 over 2-3 minutes.
[03:12] Priya: That's the kind of trace we want. Given those spikes, you'd likely need a baseline sized for ~450 qps and a burst pool for the 450->900 transient range. exact GPU math depends on model throughput — tokens/sec per GPU.
[03:26] Jordan: quick interjection: we'll share a capacity-planner spreadsheet to convert token rates to GPU counts for a few model configs (float16, int8 quant, etc).
[03:33] Carlos: great. on quantization — how much throughput uplift vs regressions in output? our ML team is sensitive to answer quality.
[03:40] Priya: Typical numbers: going from fp16 to int8 can yield 1.8-2.5x throughput improvement depending on model and kernel support; latency per token drops accordingly. quality delta is model-dependent — some models show minimal degradation on eval sets, others need calibration. Redwood's recommendations include running eval prompts to check quality and using mixed quant profiles (per-layer or selective f16 for sensitive layers). We'll provide suggested eval sets.
[04:05] Mark: Do you have experience with quantization on transformers with long-context KV caches? any gotchas?
[04:11] Priya: KV cache behavior is largely orthogonal to quantization, but when you quantize you may need extra cache-fidelity checks — e.g., numeric drift can affect logits slightly which cascades over long contexts. For long-running sessions, we recommend conservative quant settings or using higher precision for KV storage.
[04:30] Carlos: about batching — we assume batching increases GPU utilization but adds latency. how do you balance dynamic batching with latency SLOs?
[04:37] Priya: We do continuous batching with adaptive time windows. For interactive endpoints, set max batch latency budget (e.g., 20ms) and max batch size. The runtime will flush earlier if batch size hits threshold. That gives throughput gains while bounding additional batch-induced latency. For your p95 350ms SLO, we recommend target batch-add latency <= 30ms.
[05:00] Jordan: Also consider prefix caching: if many requests share similar prefixes we can serve large fraction from cache with near-zero decode cost, which reduces effective tokens/sec load on GPUs.
[05:10] Aisha: how do you warm the KV cache on cold start for on-prem? we can't stream traffic to Redwood.
[05:16] Priya: Options: 1) replay a recent trace to pre-warm cache during deployment; 2) maintain small hot-standby nodes that keep popular KV prefixes warm; 3) use a persistent KV snapshot when you persist state and load it at startup. For on-prem, persistent KV snapshot plus a quick trace replay is common. We'll provide scripts for snapshot tooling.
[05:35] Carlos: network constraints in our colo mean model fetches from private objectstore take longer — any strategies?
[05:40] Priya: Put model artifacts on local SSDs, use warm-image golden AMIs (or pre-loaded containers), and keep a minimal warm pool. Also consider quantized artifacts which are smaller and faster to fetch.
[05:52] Mark: question about admission control: if we reject low-priority requests, how do we surface that to clients gracefully?
[05:58] Jordan: we return a structured error with Retry-After and optional degraded-mode payload (e.g., cached response). For streaming UX, we can send a short 1-line fallback message so clients can display something while retrying.
[06:10] Aisha: can Redwood do per-route policies? e.g., different autoscale for embedding endpoints vs chat endpoints.
[06:15] Priya: Yes per-route model and policy. Embeddings are high-throughput and can be routed to quantized model pool, chat to dedicated low-latency pool.
[06:22] Carlos: we also need to understand billing/cost predictability when you have burst pools that are ephemeral.
[06:26] Jordan: Reserved capacity is billed predictably; burst usage is metered and billed at a premium. We'll show cost curves in the planner spreadsheet so you can trade-off reserve vs burst.
[06:36] Mark: what's the recommended cooldown/scale-down policy? we want to avoid flapping.
[06:40] Priya: Use conservative scale-down with a cool-down of 5-15 minutes depending on volatility. Quick spin-down harms cache warmness and can increase cold starts. For your workload with minute-scale spikes, I'd use 10-minute cooldown and hysteresis thresholds so you only scale down when sustained low load observed.
[06:58] Carlos: how do you measure effective concurrency? is it requests in decode stage or queued?
[07:02] Priya: effective concurrency is requests actively using decode kernels (i.e., in GPU forward/backward), not queued. We expose token-inflight metrics, queue length, and GPU utilization so you can set autoscale triggers on the metric that best correlates with your cost.
[07:14] Jordan: If helpful, we'll add derived columns in the spreadsheet: tokens/sec -> GPU count under different batch/quant configs and expected p95 latency.
[07:22] Aisha: about on-prem security: we require KMS integration and HSM for keys, plus audit logs. does Redwood support that?
[07:29] Jordan: yes. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integration, SAML SSO, RBAC and audit logs. For on-prem we ship a control-plane that runs in your VPC and an agent on the cluster; we'll share the deployment checklist.
[07:40] Mark: any specific network ports or egress we need to plan for?
[07:43] Priya: We'll send the network diagram. generally need egress to your KMS endpoints, internal registry access for model images, and optional telemetry endpoints. We can run fully air-gapped with artifact import workflow.
[07:55] Carlos: back to queueing — do you support prioritized preemption so interactive requests bump batch jobs?
[08:00] Priya: yes preemption + prioritized queues. Background jobs can be limited to leftover capacity; interactive gets priority and can preempt long-running decode jobs if configured.
[08:10] Mark: let's talk numbers quickly — assume single 80B model on A100-like equivalent gives ~X tokens/sec. do you have ballpark?
[08:17] Priya: Ballpark for 32k context 80B unquantized is low throughput; for 8k context compute around ~600-1200 tokens/sec per A100 depending on kernels. Quantized int8 might be 1.8-2x that. We'll provide model-specific benchmarks; confidence intervals vary.
[08:33] Carlos: ok we should run end-to-end benchmark including network, prefix cache misses, and cold-starts.
[08:38] Jordan: Agreed. propose: Nimbus runs a 50k request benchmark covering steady + spike phases. Redwood will run same trace on a reserved test pool to compare.
[08:48] Aisha: who owns the benchmark harness?
[08:50] Priya: Redwood can share a harness (k6 + custom trace replayer) and a runner for on-prem. we'll include instructions for collecting KV warm/cold metrics.
[08:58] Carlos: any pitfalls when using mixed fleets (some GPUs on cloud, some on-prem)?
[09:02] Priya: The main complexity is routing and fallbacks. Redwood can route requests by policy (region, cost, latency). If on-prem is overloaded we fallback to hosted but need to consider data residency and PII. Also consistent model versions/quant artifacts must be synced.
[09:18] Mark: re: fallbacks, how do you ensure output parity? model variants (quant vs unquant) might diverge.
[09:23] Priya: we recommend a fast-path quant variant for non-sensitive workloads and a gold-path full precision for regulated data. For parity-sensitive flows you can set policy to prefer gold-path; also Redwood supports A/B evaluation and drift detection alerts when variants diverge on eval sets.
[09:40] Carlos: one last operational question: what metrics should we alert on to avoid capacity surprises?
[09:44] Priya: Key alerts: sustained GPU utilization > 75% for > 2 minutes, queue length > threshold, token-inflight rate approaching provisioned token/sec capacity, KV cache hitrate drop, and cold-starts frequency > threshold. We can preconfigure dashboards.
[09:58] Jordan: Great. let's recap action items and next steps.
[10:02] Jordan: Redwood will: 1) share capacity-planner spreadsheet and sample burst policies, 2) provide quant and batch recommendations and benchmark artifacts, 3) send security & deployment checklist. Nimbus will: 1) export 72h trace and run 50k benchmark, 2) confirm networking & KMS details. We'll aim follow-up POC kickoff week of 2025-09-08.
[10:26] Mark: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:29] Carlos: thanks.
[10:32] Priya: thanks folks, we'll send the artifacts after this call.
[10:35] Jordan: bye all.
